name: access
synopsis: int faccessat(int dirfd, const char *pathname, int mode, int flags);
int syscall(SYS_faccessat2, int dirfd, const char *pathname, int mode, int flags);
description: The access() function checks whether the calling process can access the file specified by pathname using its real UID and GID, rather than effective IDs. It tests for file existence or read, write, and execute permissions as specified in mode, allowing set-user-ID programs to verify the invoking user's authority.

parameters.name: pathname
parameters.description: Path to the file to check permissions for

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Specifies the accessibility checks, such as F_OK for existence, or R_OK, W_OK, X_OK for read, write, execute permissions

parameters.name: dirfd
parameters.description: File descriptor for the directory, used by faccessat() for relative paths (AT_FDCWD for current working directory)

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Flags for faccessat() and faccessat2(), such as AT_EACCESS or AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW

return_value.success: Returns zero if all requested permissions are granted or the file exists (for F_OK)
return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set to indicate the error

errors.description: The requested access would be denied, or search permission is denied for a directory in the path
For faccessat(), pathname is relative and dirfd is not AT_FDCWD or a valid file descriptor
pathname points outside the accessible address space
mode was incorrectly specified, or invalid flag in flags for faccessat()
Too many symbolic links encountered in resolving pathname
A component of pathname does not exist or is a dangling symbolic link
A component of pathname is not a directory, or for faccessat(), pathname is relative and dirfd is not a directory
Write permission was requested for a file with the immutable flag set
Write permission was requested on a read-only filesystem
Write access was requested to an executable that is being executed

bugs: The glibc wrapper for faccessat() in versions before 2.33 does not account for ACLs and may behave incorrectly; early Linux kernels had issues with X_OK tests for superusers and ignored MS_NOEXEC mount flags before Linux 2.6.20.
versions: access(): SVr4, 4.3BSD, POSIX.1-2001; faccessat(): Linux 2.6.16, glibc 2.4; faccessat2(): Linux 5.8
